title: BRICS and the new scramble for space
gist: The author reframes BRICS space cooperation as patron-client diplomacy rather than multilateralism: China, at roughly 60% of the bloc's output, builds satellites and keeps a hand on the ground stations for Egypt, Ethiopia, Brazil, Indonesia and Bolivia bilaterally, while Washington's 71-signatory Artemis Accords run a gentler version of the same play — and the New Delhi summit will reveal whether a proposed BRICS Space Council is real multilateralism or five bilateral deals sharing a logo.

insights.claim: Beijing covered about three-quarters of the US$8 million cost of Ethiopia's ground station as a grant, tracking Ethiopia's 2019 Taiyuan-launched satellite plus a growing fleet of Chinese-built ones, with officials now describing the station as capacity Addis Ababa can resell.
insights.so_what: Grant-funded ground infrastructure is cheap influence at single-digit millions — the cost asymmetry explains why Chinese space diplomacy scales so easily.
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: China's standard model across Egypt, Ethiopia, Brazil, Indonesia and Bolivia is to build the satellite, train the operators, and retain influence over the ground station after the handover ceremony.
insights.so_what: The durable leverage sits in ground segment and operator training, not the spacecraft — the right place to look when assessing dependence in any space deal.
insights.quote: build it, train the operators, keep a hand on the ground station after the ceremony
insights.locator: Its footprint in orbit shows the same gap
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: A CSIS analysis found 64 countries engaged in Chinese space cooperation since 2000, three quarters of them from the Global South, with CSIS's Matthew Funaiole framing it as a contest over who wins the space diplomacy race there.
insights.so_what: 64 countries is the scale number for Chinese space outreach — an established network effect that Western space diplomacy is playing catch-up against.
insights.quote: this is really about who’s winning the space diplomacy race in the Global South
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: China's economy is roughly five times India's — about US$20.9 trillion against US$4.15 trillion — and makes up something like 60% of BRICS output, more if the disputed Saudi and UAE memberships are excluded.
insights.so_what: At ~60% of bloc GDP, any BRICS institution defaults to Chinese preferences unless explicitly structured against it — the base rate for reading BRICS announcements.
insights.locator: China’s economy is roughly five times India’s
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: Satellites are priced in dollars, and China alone outweighs everyone else in the bloc combined — a point that undercuts BRICS de-dollarisation framing in the space domain specifically.
insights.so_what: Even within the supposed alternative bloc, hard-asset space procurement is dollar-denominated — a reality check on de-dollarisation narratives.
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: The existing 2021 BRICS agreement links only six satellites, modest next to the bilateral deals happening around it, so the bloc's formal cooperation is thinner than its rhetoric.
insights.so_what: Six linked satellites is the measurable extent of actual BRICS space multilateralism — a useful benchmark against which to judge any new announcement.
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

themes.theme: The Space Council test at New Delhi

insights.claim: At a BRICS space agency heads meeting in Bengaluru in June 2026, members revived a Russian proposal pushed since 2024 to formalise a standing Space Council, an idea that outlived the replacement of Roscosmos's Yury Borisov.
insights.so_what: A standing Space Council is the concrete deliverable to watch at the New Delhi summit — its fate is the cleanest test of whether BRICS institutionalises or stays transactional.
insights.locator: At a BRICS space agency heads meeting in Bengaluru
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: Whether a Space Council survives the New Delhi summit, where India holds the chair, will show whether BRICS space cooperation is real multilateralism or bilateral deals dressed in a shared logo.
insights.so_what: A binary, near-dated test with an observable outcome — useful for calibrating how much weight to give BRICS institutional announcements generally.
insights.quote: five bilateral deals wearing a shared BRICS logo
insights.locator: Whether it survives the New Delhi summit
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

themes.theme: Russia and India break the pattern

insights.claim: Russia's biggest space partnership is now with Iran, with recent Iranian launches occurring while Iranian drones fly over Ukraine — a shrinking space power bartering rocket rides for drone favours rather than running a patron project.
insights.so_what: Russian space capability is now a barter chip in a war economy, not a source of bloc leadership — discount Moscow as an independent patron in space diplomacy.
insights.quote: a shrinking space power bartering rocket rides for drone favours
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: India gave its neighbours a satellite in 2017, built its own navigation system instead of joining BeiDou, and signed the Artemis Accords in 2023 — behaving less as a rival patron than as a country opting out of being anyone's client.
insights.so_what: India's refusal to join BeiDou and its Artemis signature mark it as the structural blocker to a Chinese-run BRICS space architecture.
insights.locator: India, meanwhile, gave its neighbours a satellite
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

themes.theme: Washington runs the same play, gentler

insights.claim: The Artemis Accords passed 71 signatories this year, using non-binding commitments to align signatories with American standards — the same patron impulse as China's, in a gentler wrapper, since a signature is not a decade of satellite debt.
insights.so_what: Standards alignment is the lower-cost, higher-reach influence instrument; the US approach scales faster but locks in less deeply than Chinese debt-and-hardware packages.
insights.locator: Washington runs a nearly identical operation
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: Egypt has bought satellites from Ukraine, Russia, France, Italy and China, which shows Chinese packages do not automatically trap buyers — the lock is political rather than technical.
insights.so_what: Dependence in space deals tracks a country's outside options, not the vendor's terms — assess client risk by counting available alternative suppliers.
insights.locator: That’s where the “client” label needs qualifying
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: Bolivia borrowed US$251 million from the China Development Bank against a satellite it is still paying off, and Ethiopia followed its first satellite with a second in 2020 and now a third — both stayed because they had nowhere else to stand.
insights.so_what: A US$251m satellite loan against a small economy is the concrete shape of space debt dependence — the model to watch as more Global South states enter orbit.
insights.locator: Ethiopia and Bolivia don’t have that leverage
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: Indonesia runs a Chinese satellite and training programme with an unresolved question over who controls the data, alongside an Indian tracking station on Biak dating to the 1990s, making its 'independent and active' doctrine a survival tactic rather than a principle.
insights.so_what: Data control, not hardware ownership, is the unresolved leverage point in these deals — the question to ask of any satellite partnership.
insights.quote: bank the technology, keep more than one door open, and then let yourself be fought over because being fought over beats being ignored
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo

insights.claim: BRICS is not racing the West to space but reviving the West's oldest manoeuvre — trading access for loyalty and calling it partnership — while its two biggest members trust each other too little to run that play together, producing separate deals that happen to close at the same summit.
insights.so_what: Read BRICS summit deliverables as a stack of bilateral transactions, not bloc policy — it changes what the announcements are worth.
insights.quote: BRICS isn’t racing the West to space. It’s reviving the West’s oldest manoeuvre, trading access for loyalty and calling it partnership.
insights.locator: So, BRICS isn’t racing the West to space
insights.speaker: Vania Trixie Widodo
